title: Indian Economic Development
tagline: How development is measured, planning in India, the change after liberalisation, and the challenges the economy still faces.

overview.intro: Development is not the same as growth, and the difference is the spine of this unit. A country can double its output while half its people gain nothing, which is why economists measure development through health, literacy and poverty alongside income. This unit takes the parameters of development, the role of planning in India since independence, the structural change brought by liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, the meaning of sustainable development, and the current challenges facing the Indian economy, so that the reader can judge a country’s position rather than merely quote a growth rate.

facts.label: Growth vs development
facts.value: Growth is a rise in real output or income; development is a rise in wellbeing that includes health, literacy, distribution and freedom.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: Real GDP and per capita income, literacy, life expectancy, poverty ratio, inequality, and infrastructure.

facts.label: Planning in India
facts.value: Five-year plans from 1951, with the focus moving from heavy industry to agriculture to liberalisation and then to sustainable and inclusive growth.

facts.label: 1991 reforms
facts.value: Liberalisation removed licences, privatisation allowed non-state ownership, and globalisation opened trade and capital flows.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish economic growth from economic development.
List and explain the parameters used to measure development.
Describe the role of planning in the Indian economy.
Explain liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation and their effects.
State the challenges facing the Indian economy and the idea of sustainable development.

blocks.text: Economic growth is a quantitative increase in the real output of goods and services over time, usually measured by a rise in real gross domestic product or in per capita income. Economic development is a broader quantitative and qualitative change that raises the standard of living and the wellbeing of the people, covering not only output but also its distribution, the availability of education and health, and the reduction of poverty. Growth is necessary for development, since there is nothing to redistribute if nothing is produced, but it is not sufficient: a country can post strong growth while life expectancy, literacy and nutrition stagnate for large sections.

blocks.caption: Economic growth against economic development
rows: Quantitative and qualitative change in wellbeing
Real GDP or per capita income
Composite of income, health, literacy, poverty
How the benefits are shared and sustained

items.text: An economy where growth comes entirely from oil extraction consumed by a small elite.
items.note: Output rises while most indicators of wellbeing do not, which is growth without development.

items.text: Rising school enrolment and falling infant mortality alongside moderate growth.
items.note: Development, because the gains reach people rather than only the accounts.

blocks.text: Because development is multidimensional, no single number can capture it. Real gross domestic product measures total output adjusted for price changes; per capita income divides it by the population and gives an average standard of living; the literacy rate measures the share of the population able to read and write; life expectancy at birth summarises health and nutrition; the poverty ratio shows the share living below a minimum consumption level; and the distribution of income shows how evenly the gains are spread. Infrastructure indicators such as power, transport and communication are also treated as parameters because they condition every other gain.

blocks.caption: Parameters and what each reveals
rows: Size and pace of output growth
Depth of poverty among those counted

items: Human Development Index combines income, health and education into one figure.
A composite measure corrects the worst blind spots of any single indicator.
Comparisons between countries need the same base year and definitions.
Rising average income with falling life expectancy signals distribution failure.

learn.title: Planning in India and the change after 1991

blocks.text: India has been planning since the First Five Year Plan of 1951, and the direction of that planning moved with the country’s problems. The early plans emphasised agriculture and irrigation because the immediate crisis was food security, the second and third waves emphasised heavy industry and capital goods on the model of a self-reliant industrial base, and later plans turned to poverty removal, employment and rural development. The Planning Commission was replaced in 2015 by NITI Aayog, which shifted the role from allocating plan funds to fostering cooperative federalism and providing strategic policy advice.

The reforms of 1991 came from a balance of payments crisis in which foreign exchange reserves had fallen to a matter of weeks of imports. The response was liberalisation, which dismantled the licence raj and freed firms to produce and expand without prior permission; privatisation, which allowed non-state ownership and disinvestment in public sector enterprises; and globalisation, which reduced tariffs, opened the capital account and integrated India with world markets. The gains are visible in higher growth, wider consumer choice, foreign investment and a large service sector; the costs include pressure on small firms that could not compete, greater exposure to world price movements, and a widening of inequality between the skilled and the unskilled.

blocks.caption: Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation
rows: Licences abolished, entry and expansion freed
Closure of inefficient units and job loss
Disinvestment and space for private and foreign ownership
Risk of public objectives being diluted
Tariffs cut, trade and capital flows opened

blocks.text: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It requires three conditions to hold together: economic viability, social equity and environmental protection. A growth path that depletes groundwater, degrades soil or loads the atmosphere with emissions may show strong figures now and leave the next generation poorer, which is why environmental cost must be counted rather than treated as free.

blocks.caption: Current challenges facing the Indian economy
rows: A large population near the subsistence level and a wide spread of incomes
Seasonal, educated and disguised unemployment persisting alongside job creation
Small holdings, monsoon dependence, low farm incomes and weak market access
Malnutrition, uneven health access and learning outcomes below enrolment
Power, logistics and digital access still constraining growth in many regions
Air and water pollution, resource depletion and climate vulnerability

items: Growth must be inclusive, so that employment and incomes rise together.
Agriculture needs productivity, irrigation and reliable market access.
Human capital must rise with output, or growth cannot be sustained.
Environmental costs should be priced rather than ignored.
Reforms must protect small firms and workers while raising efficiency.

keyPoints: Economic growth is a rise in output; economic development is a rise in wellbeing across dimensions.
Growth is necessary for development but does not guarantee it.
Parameters include real GDP, per capita income, literacy, life expectancy, poverty and inequality.
Each parameter has a blind spot, which is why composite indices are used.
India has planned since 1951, moving from agriculture to heavy industry to inclusive growth.
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.
The 1991 reforms were liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, triggered by a balance of payments crisis.
The reforms raised growth and choice while increasing competition pressure and inequality.
Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations.
Current challenges are poverty, unemployment, agricultural distress, human development gaps, infrastructure and environment.
examFocus: Growth and development questions are marked on the distinction plus one example of each, not on definitions alone.
Parameters questions should name the parameter, what it reveals and what it conceals.
Reform answers should give benefit and cost together, since balanced treatment carries the marks.

vocabulary.meaning: Quantitative increase in the real output of goods and services over time.
Broad improvement in wellbeing including health, education, distribution and freedom.
National income divided by the population, giving an average income per person.
Deliberate allocation of resources over a period to achieve stated objectives.
Removal of controls and licences so that firms decide output and investment freely.
Integration of an economy with the world through trade, capital and technology flows.
Development that meets present needs without compromising future generations.

questions.prompt: Economic development differs from economic growth in that:
options: Development is a quantitative rise in output only
Development includes qualitative change in wellbeing, not only output
Growth includes distribution while development does not
Development is always faster than growth
questions.answer: Development includes qualitative change in wellbeing, not only output
questions.explanation: Development covers income plus health, education, distribution and other dimensions, whereas growth measures output alone.

questions.prompt: Which indicator is NOT a parameter of economic development?
questions.explanation: Factory registration is an administrative count that reveals nothing about output, health, education or distribution.

questions.prompt: The reforms of 1991 in India were principally a response to:
options: A fall in the rate of inflation
A severe balance of payments crisis
A decision to leave the World Trade Organisation
questions.answer: A severe balance of payments crisis
questions.explanation: Foreign exchange reserves had fallen to barely a few weeks of imports, which forced the liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation package.

options: Economic viability, social equity and environmental protection
questions.answer: Economic viability, social equity and environmental protection
questions.explanation: The three pillars are economic, social and environmental, and development fails if any one is sacrificed for the others.

questions.prompt: The body that replaced the Planning Commission in 2015 and advises on strategy is called __________ Aayog.
questions.explanation: NITI Aayog changed the role from allocating plan funds to fostering cooperative federalism and strategic policy advice.

questions.prompt: The rise in the real output of goods and services over time, measured by real GDP, is called economic __________ .
questions.explanation: Growth is the quantitative part; development is the wider change that includes how the gains are shared.

questions.prompt: State four parameters used to measure economic development.
questions.answer: Four parameters are real gross domestic product, which measures the size and pace of output; per capita income, which gives average income per person; the literacy rate, which measures access to basic education; and life expectancy at birth, which summarises health and nutrition. The poverty ratio and the distribution of income are also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each parameter needs a line on what it reveals, since naming indicators without explaining them earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: Explain the three components of the 1991 reforms with one benefit and one cost of each.
questions.answer: Liberalisation removed industrial licences so firms could produce and expand freely, raising efficiency and investment, at the cost of closures and job losses among inefficient units. Privatisation allowed non-state ownership and disinvestment in public sector firms, bringing capital, technology and management skill, at the risk of diluting public objectives. Globalisation cut tariffs and opened trade and capital flows, giving consumers choice and exporters access to world markets, while exposing domestic industry to competition from abroad. The three together are usually described as LPG reforms.
questions.explanation: All three components are needed with a benefit and a cost attached to each, since unbalanced answers lose marks.

questions.prompt: Explain sustainable development and state the challenges facing the Indian economy.
questions.answer: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, and it requires economic viability, social equity and environmental protection to hold together. A path that grows output by depleting groundwater or loading the atmosphere with emissions transfers the cost to the future and fails the test. The challenges facing India are persistent poverty and inequality of income; unemployment and underemployment including educated and seasonal unemployment; agricultural distress from small holdings, monsoon dependence and low farm incomes; human development gaps in nutrition, health access and learning outcomes; infrastructure and energy constraints in power, logistics and digital access; and environmental pressure from pollution, resource depletion and climate vulnerability. Each of these limits the sustainability of growth, because output cannot keep rising if the workforce is unhealthy, the land is degraded or the infrastructure is saturated.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the definition with its three conditions and at least four challenges explained rather than listed.

questions.prompt: A state reports 9% real GDP growth for a year, yet its malnutrition rate rose and rural employment fell. Analyse the figures using the growth and development distinction and recommend what the state should measure next.
questions.answer: The state has recorded growth, which is a quantitative rise in real output, but the development indicators moved backwards: malnutrition rising shows that the gains did not reach household consumption of food, and rural employment falling shows that the growth was not labour-absorbing, probably because it came from capital-intensive or service activity. On the growth and development distinction this is growth without development, and per capita income alone would have concealed it because the average can rise while the lower half loses. The state should next measure a set rather than a single figure: the poverty ratio and the rural employment rate to see who is gaining, the literacy and life expectancy figures to capture human development, and the distribution of income to check whether the spread is widening. It should also track a composite measure such as the Human Development Index for its own state, because a composite corrects the blind spot of output, and it should publish these alongside GDP so that policy responds to wellbeing and not only to output.
questions.explanation: Marks are for applying the distinction correctly, explaining why the average misleads, and recommending a specific set of indicators with a reason for each.
